analogy.p: Imagine the whole school register is the universal set ξ. Drama club and choir are two sets, drawn as circles. A student in both clubs sits in the overlap (A ∩ B); a student in neither club is still on the register, so lives outside the circles but inside the rectangle. If the head teacher picks a student at random from the register, probability is the count in the region divided by the whole register. If the head teacher says 'pick a student from the choir', the register shrinks to the choir list: that is conditional probability, with the choir as the new total. The analogy breaks down because real clubs change membership over time, while in a probability question the sets are fixed and every item sits in exactly one region.

bullets: The **universal set**, ξ, is every item being considered in the problem. It is drawn as a rectangle, and every number or element must be somewhere inside it, even if it belongs to no circle.

Each **set** is a collection of items with something in common (a property such as 'plays tennis' or 'is a multiple of 3'). A set is drawn as a circle or oval and is labelled with a capital letter such as A or B.

Items are called **elements** or **members** of a set. In a Venn diagram of numbers, the elements are written inside the circle; in a probability Venn diagram you more often write the **number of items** in each region.
A Venn diagram can show elements (for example 2, 4, 6) or frequencies (for example 12 students). The question tells you which; always read the key carefully.
A region outside every circle but inside the rectangle is still part of ξ. It holds the items that are in none of the sets, and forgetting it is the single most common reason a total comes out wrong.
Two circles that do not overlap at all mean the sets are **mutually exclusive** (nothing is in both). Two overlapping circles mean some items are in both.
Venn diagrams are named after John Venn, who introduced them in the 1880s, but you do not need history in an exam; you need accurate labelling and counting.
core.h: What a Venn diagram is and why it is used
core.p: A **Venn diagram** is a picture that shows how groups of things (called **sets**) overlap. Everything under consideration sits inside a rectangle called the **universal set**, written ξ (the Greek letter xi). Each set is drawn as a circle inside the rectangle, and where two circles overlap the diagram shows the things that belong to both sets. Venn diagrams are useful because they turn a wordy problem about groups (for example students who play football and/or tennis) into a visual map, so that counting, probability and conditional probability become reading and adding numbers in regions. On the Edexcel specification you must be able to construct, interpret and use Venn diagrams with set notation, and to use them to find probabilities including conditional probabilities.

bullets: **ξ** is the universal set (everything in the problem). **∅** or **{ }** is the **empty set**, the set with no elements.
**x ∈ A** is read 'x is an element of A' (x is in A). **x ∉ A** is read 'x is not an element of A'.
**A ∪ B** is the **union** of A and B: all elements in A or in B or in both (think U for 'unite'). It is the whole area covered by both circles.
**A ∩ B** is the **intersection** of A and B: only the elements in both A and B (the overlapping lens). Think 'and'.
**A'** (also written A with a dash, or Aᶜ) is the **complement** of A: all elements of ξ that are not in A. It includes the area outside both circles.
**n(A)** means the **number of elements** in A. So n(A ∪ B) is the number of elements in the union and n(ξ) is the total in the whole diagram.
**A ⊂ B** means A is a **subset** of B: every element of A is also in B. On a Venn diagram, circle A sits wholly inside circle B.

A set can be written by listing its elements in curly brackets, for example A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, or by a rule, for example A = {x : x is an even number less than 10}, read 'the set of x such that x is an even number less than 10'.
core.h: Set notation you must know (reading the symbols)
core.p: Exam questions use a small shorthand called **set notation** to describe regions of a Venn diagram, so you need to read it as quickly as you read words. The symbols come in three groups: those that describe membership of a set (∈ and ∉), those that combine or complement sets (∪, ∩ and the dash for complement) and those that count or compare sets (n(A), ⊂ and ∅). The idea is that each symbol is a short way of writing a phrase such as 'or', 'and' or 'not'. Learn them with a one-word reading each, because mark schemes award marks for correct use of the notation as well as for the answer.

bullets: Region 1, **A only** (in A but not in B), is written A ∩ B'. In the figure with ξ = 40 it contains 12 students.
Region 2, **both A and B**, is A ∩ B. It sits in the overlap and contains 6 students.
Region 3, **B only** (in B but not in A), is B ∩ A'. It contains 8 students.
Region 4, **neither**, is (A ∪ B)' and is also A' ∩ B'. It lies outside both circles and contains 14 students.
The whole circle A is regions 1 and 2 together, so n(A) = 12 + 6 = 18. Similarly n(B) = 6 + 8 = 14.
A ∪ B is regions 1, 2 and 3, so n(A ∪ B) = 12 + 6 + 8 = 26. The complement (A ∪ B)' is region 4: 40 − 26 = 14.
A' is everything not in A, which is regions 3 and 4, so n(A') = 8 + 14 = 22. Check: n(A) + n(A') = 18 + 22 = 40 = n(ξ).
The four region counts always add up to n(ξ). Use this as a built-in check on any Venn diagram you fill in.
core.h: Reading a two-set Venn diagram: the four regions
core.p: Two overlapping circles divide the rectangle into **four regions**, and every item in ξ lies in exactly one of them. These are: in A only, in both A and B (the intersection), in B only, and in neither (outside both circles). Being able to name the four regions in both words and set notation is the foundation of everything else in this topic. A frequent trap is that the number 'in A' (n(A)) includes the intersection, so the label on a Venn diagram showing 'A only' is smaller than n(A). Always ask yourself whether a number refers to a whole circle or to one region of it.

bullets: Step 1: draw the rectangle labelled ξ, draw the circles overlapping (even if you think they might not overlap, draw them overlapping unless told they are mutually exclusive) and label each circle with its set name and meaning.
Step 2: put the **intersection** number in first. If the question says '6 play both', write 6 in the lens. If no overlap number is given, use algebra or the union formula to find it.
Step 3: find the 'only' regions by subtracting the intersection from each circle's total. Football 18, both 6, so A only = 18 − 6 = 12. Tennis 14, both 6, so B only = 14 − 6 = 8.
Step 4: add the three region counts to get n(A ∪ B) = 12 + 6 + 8 = 26. The remainder of the total goes outside the circles: 40 − 26 = 14 play neither sport.
Step 5: **check**: all four regions add up to n(ξ). If it does not, find the error before answering any probability question.
If the question gives you the number in neither and the total, you can work out n(A ∪ B) = n(ξ) − n(neither) first, then use n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) rearranged to find the overlap.
If the numbers do not seem to fit (a region would be negative) re-read the question: you may have used a circle total as an 'only' value.
Tip: write the region labels in pencil lightly at first (A only, both, B only, neither) so you do not mix them up.
core.h: Constructing a Venn diagram from information (the working-inwards method)
core.p: To fill in a Venn diagram from a worded problem, always work from the **inside outwards**: start with the overlap (the most 'specific' piece of information, such as 'both'), then work out the 'only' regions by subtraction, and finally use the total to find the 'neither' region. This order works because the figures given in a question usually include the overlap, for example '18 play football' means 18 in total in circle A, not 18 in the A-only region. If you write 18 in the A-only region you double-count the students who play both. Good Venn solutions show the subtraction clearly so that method marks can be awarded even if an arithmetic slip happens.

bullets: **A ∪ B**: shade the whole of both circles (regions 1, 2 and 3). Words: 'in A or B or both'.
**A ∩ B**: shade only the lens where the circles overlap (region 2). Words: 'in A and in B'.
**A'**: shade everything in the rectangle that is outside circle A, including the part of circle B that is not in A (regions 3 and 4).
**(A ∪ B)'**: shade only the area outside both circles (region 4). Words: 'in neither A nor B'.
**A ∩ B'**: in A and not in B, which is region 1 (A only). The dash applies to B only because it follows B directly.

**A' ∩ B'** is the same region as (A ∪ B)' (region 4), and **A' ∪ B'** is the same region as (A ∩ B)', which is everything except the lens. These equivalences are known as **De Morgan's laws**; you will not normally be asked to name them, but they explain why the brackets matter.
Brackets change the answer: (A ∪ B)' is just region 4 but A ∪ B' includes region 4 as well as all of A. Always check where the dash sits.
If a question asks you to 'describe the shaded region using set notation', find a notation that fits exactly the shaded regions, then test it region by region.
core.h: Shading regions and matching set notation to regions
core.p: A common exam task is to **shade the region** described by a piece of set notation, or to write the notation for a shaded region. The method is to translate the notation into words, one symbol at a time: ∪ means 'or', ∩ means 'and' and the dash means 'not'. Then decide which of the four regions satisfy the words. The figure shows four core examples. The trickiest are the complements: A' is the whole rectangle except circle A, and (A ∪ B)' is only the area outside both circles. Practise by shading with a pencil or a light diagonal hatch so that you can see overlaps clearly.

bullets: The eight regions in the figure with ξ = 36 are: A only 8, B only 6, C only 5, A and B only 4, A and C only 3, B and C only 2, all three 1, none 7. They add to 36.
To find the total in a **circle**, add the four regions that make it up. n(A) = A only + (A and B only) + (A and C only) + all three = 8 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 16.
To find a **pairwise intersection** such as A ∩ B, include the centre: n(A ∩ B) = 4 + 1 = 5. The 'only' version (A and B but not C) is A ∩ B ∩ C'.

**Method for filling in**: (1) centre first, (2) subtract the centre from each given pairwise overlap to find 'exactly two', (3) subtract the centre and both 'exactly two' regions from each circle total to find 'only', (4) total minus the sum of all seven circle regions gives 'neither'.
A union of three sets, A ∪ B ∪ C, is every region except 'neither'. Here it is 36 − 7 = 29 elements.

The inclusion–exclusion formula n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(A∩C) − n(B∩C) + n(A∩B∩C) is not required in the Edexcel GCSE, but it helps you check: 16 + 13 + 11 − 5 − 4 − 3 + 1 = 29 ✓ (n(A∩C) = 3 + 1 = 4 and n(B∩C) = 2 + 1 = 3).
Label each circle clearly and draw the circles large enough to write numbers in every region, including the small ones. Untidy diagrams are a major cause of lost marks.
Condition words help locate regions: 'at least two' = the three 'exactly two' regions and the centre; 'exactly one' = the three 'only' regions; 'all three' = the centre.
core.p: With three overlapping circles A, B and C the rectangle is split into **eight regions**: three 'only' regions, three regions where exactly two circles overlap, one region in the centre where all three overlap, and the region outside all circles. The same inside-out principle applies, with a twist: start in the **centre** (A ∩ B ∩ C), then fill in the regions where exactly two sets overlap by subtracting the centre from each pairwise overlap, then the 'only' regions, then 'neither'. Questions at Higher tier often give totals such as n(A ∩ B) which include the centre, so you must subtract the centre to get the 'exactly two' region.

bullets: **P(A) = n(A) ÷ n(ξ)** = (12 + 6) ÷ 40 = 18/40 = 9/20. The numerator is the whole of circle A, including the overlap.
**P(A ∩ B) = n(A ∩ B) ÷ n(ξ)** = 6/40 = 3/20. Only the lens counts.
**P(A ∪ B) = n(A ∪ B) ÷ n(ξ)** = 26/40 = 13/20. Count the three regions that are in A or B or both.
**P(neither) = P((A ∪ B)')** = 14/40 = 7/20. This is the outside region.
**P(A only)** = P(A ∩ B') = 12/40 = 3/10. This is not the same as P(A) because it excludes the overlap.
Always use the **total of the whole diagram** (including those in neither) as the denominator unless the question says 'given that', which changes the denominator (see conditional probability).
If probabilities are given on the diagram (for example 0.3, 0.1, 0.4 and 0.2), they must add to 1 and you use them exactly like counts.
Write fractions in simplest form unless the question wants a particular denominator; leaving 18/40 unsimplified is usually accepted but 9/20 is safer.
core.h: Using a Venn diagram to find probabilities
core.p: When a Venn diagram shows counts, probabilities come directly from it. For equally likely outcomes, **P(event) = number of outcomes in the event ÷ total number of outcomes**. In Venn language this is **P(A) = n(A) ÷ n(ξ)**. The key skill is deciding which regions belong to the event and adding their counts for the numerator, while the denominator is the total in the universal set (the sum of all regions, including 'neither'). Probabilities should be given as a fraction in its simplest form (or as a decimal or percentage) and must lie between 0 and 1. The figure shows the same diagram with each count written over 40.

bullets: **General rule**: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Check with the figure: 18/40 + 14/40 − 6/40 = 26/40 ✓.
**Rearranged** to find the overlap: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B). This is how you find the number in both when you know the union from the 'neither' value.

**Mutually exclusive events** have no overlap: P(A ∩ B) = 0, circles do not overlap on the Venn diagram, and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Example: on one roll of a die, 'a 2' and 'a 5' are mutually exclusive.
**Exhaustive events** between them cover all possibilities, so P(A ∪ B) = 1. If events are both mutually exclusive and exhaustive their probabilities sum to 1.
If a question says 'events A and B are mutually exclusive' and gives P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.45, then P(A or B) = 0.75 and P(neither) = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25.
The same idea works with counts: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Using counts (40 students) is often less error-prone than decimals.
In an exam, write the rule, substitute and calculate; showing the formula earns the method mark even if the arithmetic goes wrong.
core.h: The addition rule for probability and mutually exclusive events
core.p: To find the probability that A or B happens (A ∪ B) from probabilities alone you need the **addition rule**: **P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)**. The reason you subtract is that P(A) and P(B) each include the overlap, so adding them counts the overlap twice, and it must be taken off once. On the Venn diagram this is simply the fact that the union is the two circles with the lens counted only once. If A and B are **mutually exclusive** (they cannot happen together) then P(A ∩ B) = 0 and the rule simplifies to P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Edexcel questions often ask you to use this rule to find a missing probability, usually the intersection.

bullets: **P(A') = 1 − P(A)**. In the figure, P(A) = 18/40 so P(A') = 22/40 = 11/20, which equals adding the B-only and neither regions: (8 + 14)/40.
**P(neither A nor B) = 1 − P(A ∪ B)**. In the figure that is 1 − 26/40 = 14/40.
**P(not both) = 1 − P(A ∩ B)**. The event 'not both' includes everything except the lens: 1 − 6/40 = 34/40 = 17/20.
**Exactly one** of A, B is the two 'only' regions: P = P(A only) + P(B only) = 12/40 + 8/40 = 20/40 = 1/2. Do not confuse 'exactly one' with 'at least one' (A ∪ B).
Be careful with 'not A' versus 'B': the complement A' includes both the B-only region and the neither region.
Use the complement whenever 'at least one' appears: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). It saves adding many regions.
A and A' are always mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so P(A) + P(A') = 1 exactly.
core.p: The **complement** of an event A is the event 'A does not happen', written A'. Because A either happens or does not happen, and the two cannot both happen, **P(A') = 1 − P(A)**. This is powerful because the complement is often easier to count, especially for phrases like 'at least one', 'not both' or 'neither'. On a Venn diagram, the complement is simply everything in ξ outside the set, so you can either add up the relevant regions or subtract the set from the total. For two sets, the result P((A ∪ B)') = 1 − P(A ∪ B) is used constantly to find the probability of neither.

bullets: **Recipe**: (1) identify the 'given' set, the one after the vertical bar; (2) the denominator is the **total in that set** (all regions of that circle); (3) the numerator is the part of that set that also satisfies the other event (usually the lens); (4) write as a simplified fraction.
Figure example: P(A | B) = n(A ∩ B) ÷ n(B) = 6 ÷ (6 + 8) = 6/14 = 3/7. The 40 and the outside regions play no part.
**Order matters**: P(B | A) = n(A ∩ B) ÷ n(A) = 6/18 = 1/3, which is not the same as P(A | B) = 3/7. Always check which set is the 'given' one.
In wording: 'Given that a student plays tennis, what is the probability they play football?' has 'tennis' as the given set (B) so the denominator is n(B).
Other phrases signalling conditional probability: 'if', 'of those who', 'one student is chosen from those who...', 'what fraction of the tennis players...'.
From probabilities rather than counts: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B). For example if P(A ∩ B) = 0.15 and P(B) = 0.35 then P(A | B) = 0.15 ÷ 0.35 = 3/7.
A useful rearrangement is P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B), which connects Venn diagrams to tree diagrams (you multiply along the branches).
A wrong denominator is the most common error: using 40 (the whole of ξ) instead of the size of the given set.
core.h: Conditional probability from a Venn diagram (Higher tier)
core.p: **Conditional probability** is the probability that one event happens **given that** another event has already happened. It is written **P(A | B)**, read 'the probability of A given B'. The key idea is that knowing B has happened changes the **sample space**: instead of the whole universal set, you are now only looking at the elements of B. On a Venn diagram this means you ignore everything outside circle B, and the denominator becomes n(B) rather than n(ξ). The numerator is the part of B that is also in A, that is, the intersection. This gives the formula **P(A | B) = n(A ∩ B) ÷ n(B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B)**.

bullets: **Test for independence**: compute P(A) × P(B) and compare with P(A ∩ B). In the figure, P(A) × P(B) = 18/40 × 14/40 = 252/1600 = 0.1575 but P(A ∩ B) = 6/40 = 0.15. They are not equal, so football and tennis are **not independent** for these students.
**Test using conditional probability**: if P(A | B) = P(A) the events are independent. Here P(A | B) = 3/7 ≈ 0.43 while P(A) = 9/20 = 0.45: not equal (so again not independent).
**Mutually exclusive** events are drawn as non-overlapping circles. A single die roll: 'even' and 'prime' overlap (2), but 'even' and 'odd' do not overlap.
**Independent** events are about the process (for example two separate coin tosses) and need no overlap; two circles representing independent events will normally overlap.
If two events are mutually exclusive and both have non-zero probability, they cannot be independent. Quote this reasoning if asked 'Are A and B independent?'
State your conclusion in a sentence: 'P(A) × P(B) ≠ P(A ∩ B), so the events are not independent'. A statement without numbers does not earn full marks.
Real-world data rarely gives exact equality, so questions are usually set with numbers that either match exactly or clearly differ.
core.h: Independent and mutually exclusive events: do not confuse them
core.p: Two events are **independent** if the occurrence of one has no effect on the probability of the other. In probability notation this means **P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B)**, or equivalently P(A | B) = P(A). Two events are **mutually exclusive** if they cannot happen at the same time, meaning P(A ∩ B) = 0. These are completely different ideas and, except in the trivial case where one event has probability 0, mutually exclusive events are **not** independent: if A has happened, then B definitely cannot have happened, so one event does affect the other. Higher tier questions may ask you to show whether two events are independent using a Venn diagram, by comparing P(A ∩ B) with P(A) × P(B).

bullets: Set up regions in terms of one unknown, usually the **intersection** x. Then A only = n(A) − x, B only = n(B) − x, and neither is given or found.
Form the equation: (n(A) − x) + x + (n(B) − x) + neither = n(ξ). This simplifies to n(A) + n(B) − x + neither = n(ξ).
Example: ξ = 60, n(P) = 30, n(B) = 25, neither = 10. Then 30 + 25 − x + 10 = 60, so 65 − x = 60 and x = 5.

When the regions are written as algebra such as 2x, x + 3 and 4 − x, add them all, set equal to the total, solve, and then substitute back into **every** region to check all values are non-negative integers.
Look for 'a probability from the diagram' questions that need x first: find x by the total, then substitute to find the probability.
If a ratio is given (for example the number playing only A to the number playing only B is 2 : 3), write them as 2k and 3k and form an equation as before.
Show every line of algebra; marks are usually awarded for forming the equation (M1), solving it (M1) and the final answer (A1).
core.h: Problems with algebra in a Venn diagram (Higher tier)
core.p: Some Higher tier questions put **algebraic expressions** in the regions of a Venn diagram and ask you to form and solve an equation. The idea is the same as with numbers: the regions must add up to the total in ξ, and the expressions for circle totals must match the given information. For example, if both is x, then A only is (n(A) − x) and B only is (n(B) − x). Write the sum of all regions equal to the total, simplify, and solve. Always check that your answer gives non-negative numbers in every region and that it makes sense in the context (for example, a count cannot be a fraction).

bullets: A two-way table and a two-set Venn diagram hold the same information: A and B = intersection cell, A not B = A only cell, and so on. The row/column totals correspond to n(A), n(B) and n(ξ).

A tree diagram for the same example starts with A or A' then branches to B or B' with conditional probabilities: P(A) = 18/40, then P(B | A) = 6/18. The product 18/40 × 6/18 = 6/40 is the intersection.
In a Venn diagram, conditional probability is read by **restricting to a circle**; in a tree it is read from the second set of branches; in a table it is read from a row or column.
Command words: **'Work out'** needs a numerical answer with working, **'Show that'** needs complete working leading to the stated answer, and **'Explain'** requires a reason in words.

A good exam routine: label ξ and every circle, fill in the intersection first, use subtraction for the 'only' regions, check the total, then read the probability from the diagram with the correct denominator.
Always state the probability as a fraction, decimal or percentage in line with the question, and never exceed 1 or go below 0.
Practise past Edexcel papers: Venn diagrams often appear in the later (harder) questions of Paper 2 and Paper 3 for conditional probability and with algebra at grades 7 to 9.
core.h: Linking Venn diagrams to other probability representations and exam strategy
core.p: Venn diagrams are one of several ways to organise probability information, and in exams you may choose or be told which to use. **Two-way tables** are equivalent to two-set Venn diagrams: the cells of the table correspond to the four regions. **Tree diagrams** show sequences of events and are better for dependent events with stages. **Frequency trees** work with counts rather than probabilities. A Venn diagram is the best representation when the question talks about groups, 'both', 'either' or 'neither', and when overlap matters. Being fluent in converting between them lets you check an answer using a second method, which is a good habit.

exam: **1 mark** questions: read a value from the diagram, name a region in words or write simple notation. Quote the number exactly and include units/context if asked.
**2 marks** for a probability from a completed Venn diagram: 1 mark for the correct numerator or denominator, 1 mark for the full fraction (and simplifying if required).

**3 marks** for completing a Venn from worded information: usually 1 mark for the intersection, 1 for the 'only' regions by subtraction, 1 for the 'neither' region from the total. Always show the subtractions.

**4 mark conditional probability**: 1 for the correct denominator (size of the given set), 1 for the numerator, 1 for the fraction, 1 for simplification or correct decimal. Say 'given that' reasoning in words if it helps.

**Command words**: 'Work out' (numerical answer with working), 'Show that' (full working to reach the stated value, then conclude), 'Explain' (a reason in words), 'Complete' (fill the diagram, not just the answer).
Write **set notation** accurately: ∪ for 'or', ∩ for 'and', a dash for 'not'. Examiners reward correct symbols and penalise mixing ∪ and ∩.

For a **6 mark** algebra Venn question: define the unknown, write each region in terms of x, form the equation from the total, solve, check each region is non-negative, then answer the probability asked.
Test of independence: calculate P(A) × P(B) and P(A ∩ B) as numbers, state if they are equal or not, and then write a conclusion sentence.
Model phrase: 'Given that the student plays tennis, the sample space is the 14 tennis players, of whom 6 play football, so the probability is 6/14 = 3/7.'
Check the total: the sum of the regions equals n(ξ). Do this before moving on, since an error here spoils all later answers.
Give probabilities as simplified fractions or exact decimals unless told to round; if you round, give at least 3 significant figures or follow the instructions.

mistakes.r: Circle totals include the overlap. Put the intersection in first, then A only = 18 − 6 = 12.
mistakes.w: Writing the total for a circle (for example 18) in the A-only region.

mistakes.r: The universal set includes those in neither set. All regions must add to n(ξ) and this total is the denominator.
mistakes.w: Leaving out the region outside the circles when finding a total or a probability.

mistakes.r: The denominator is n(B), the size of the given set. Restrict to the circle after the bar.
mistakes.w: Using n(ξ) as the denominator in a conditional probability such as P(A | B).

mistakes.r: The set after the bar is the given one and gives the denominator. P(A | B) = 6/14 but P(B | A) = 6/18.
mistakes.w: Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A).

mistakes.r: Brackets matter: (A ∪ B)' is only the outside region; A ∪ B' is all of A plus the outside region.
mistakes.w: Shading A ∪ B' as if it were (A ∪ B)'.

mistakes.r: Use P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) unless the events are mutually exclusive.
mistakes.w: Adding P(A) and P(B) to get P(A or B) when the events overlap.

mistakes.r: They are different ideas: mutually exclusive means P(A ∩ B) = 0; independent means P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Both with non-zero probabilities is impossible.
mistakes.w: Saying mutually exclusive events are independent.

mistakes.r: n(A ∩ B) includes the centre. Subtract the centre to get the region of A and B only.
mistakes.w: In a three-set Venn, using a pairwise total such as n(A ∩ B) as the exactly-two region.

mistakes.r: Probabilities are fractions, decimals or percentages between 0 and 1 (6/14 = 3/7).
mistakes.w: Giving a probability as a ratio such as 6 : 14 or as a number above 1.

summary: You must be able to construct and interpret Venn diagrams with two or three sets, use set notation (ξ, ∪, ∩, complement, n(A), ∈, ∅) and use the diagrams to calculate probabilities, including P(A ∪ B) and conditional probabilities (Higher tier). It matters because Venn diagrams are a reliable way to organise group information and appear in the harder questions on Edexcel Paper 2 and Paper 3.

terms.d: A collection of distinct objects or numbers, called elements or members, that share a defined property.
The set containing all the elements under consideration in a given problem; drawn as the rectangle in a Venn diagram.
An individual object belonging to a set. x ∈ A means x is an element of A.
The set of all elements that are in A, or in B, or in both.
The set of elements that are in both A and B.
The set of elements of the universal set that are not in A.
The set that contains no elements; also written { }.
A set every element of which is also an element of B.
The number of elements in set A.
Events that cannot happen at the same time, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
A set of events that between them include all possible outcomes, so their probabilities add up to 1.
Events where the outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
The probability of an event given that another event has already occurred, P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B).
The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment; in a Venn diagram it is the universal set (or the given set for conditional probability).
A diagram using overlapping circles inside a rectangle to show the relationships between sets.

worked.q: (5 marks) 40 students were asked about sports. 18 play football (F), 14 play tennis (T) and 6 play both. (a) Draw a Venn diagram to show this. (b) One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student plays neither sport. (c) A student is chosen at random from those who play tennis. Find the probability that they also play football.
steps: (a) Both = 6 goes in the overlap. Football only = 18 − 6 = 12. Tennis only = 14 − 6 = 8.
Number playing at least one sport = 12 + 6 + 8 = 26, so neither = 40 − 26 = 14 (outside the circles).
(c) 'Given tennis' restricts the sample space to the 14 tennis players (6 + 8). Of these, 6 also play football.

worked.q: (4 marks) ξ = 60 people. 30 like pizza (P), 25 like burgers (B) and 10 like neither. (a) Work out how many like both. (b) Find P(B | P), the probability that a person who likes pizza also likes burgers.
steps: (a) Number who like at least one = 60 − 10 = 50.
Check the regions: P only 25, both 5, B only 20, neither 10; 25 + 5 + 20 + 10 = 60 ✓.
(b) Given pizza, the sample space is the 30 who like pizza. Of them 5 also like burgers.

worked.q: (4 marks) The Venn diagram shows ξ = 36 students with A only 8, B only 6, C only 5, A and B only 4, A and C only 3, B and C only 2, all three 1, none 7. (a) Find P(A ∪ B). (b) Find P(C' | A), the probability that a student in A is not in C.
steps: (a) A ∪ B contains every region in A or B: 8 + 4 + 3 + 1 (circle A) plus 6 + 2 (B only and B and C only) = 16 + 8 = 24.
(b) Given A, the sample space is the 16 in circle A. Those not in C are A only (8) and A and B only (4): 12.
